questions.scenario: A buggy commit that changed fee rounding was merged to main yesterday and deployed. Several other commits have been merged since.
questions.question: How should you undo it?
options: git reset --hard to before the commit and force-push main
Edit the old commit with git commit --amend
Delete the main branch and recreate it
git revert <sha> on a branch, review and merge it, so a new commit reverses the change without rewriting shared history
questions.explanation: Rewriting history on a shared branch breaks everyone's clones and loses later work. Revert adds a reversing commit that goes through the normal review and deployment flow.

questions.scenario: You rebased your own feature branch onto the latest main and now need to update the remote branch.
questions.question: Which push command is appropriate?
options: Delete the remote branch and push to a new name every time
git push --force
git push origin main --force
git push --force-with-lease
questions.explanation: Rebasing rewrites your branch's commits, so a forced update is needed. --force-with-lease refuses if someone else pushed to the branch since you last fetched, protecting their work.

questions.scenario: During a rebase you hit a conflict on the VAT_RATE constant: main changed the value's formatting and your branch added a rounding constant next to it.
questions.question: What is the correct way to resolve it?
options: Always choose your own version
Abort and copy your files over main manually
Always choose main's version
Understand both changes, combine them correctly, remove the markers, run the tests, then git add and git rebase --continue
questions.explanation: Conflict resolution must preserve both intentions and be verified, because a resolution can compile and still be wrong.

questions.scenario: After an accidental git reset --hard HEAD~3 on your local branch, three unpushed commits seem to be gone.
questions.question: How can you recover them?
options: Use git reflog to find the commit the branch pointed to before the reset, then reset or branch to it
Run git revert HEAD~3
They are permanently deleted; rewrite the code
Clone the repository again
questions.explanation: The reflog records where HEAD and branches pointed recently, so commits remain reachable for some time after a reset.

questions.scenario: You are configuring protection for main in a payments repository.
questions.question: Which rules support the bank's change-control requirements? (Choose two.)
options: Allow administrators to push directly to main in emergencies
Allow force pushes so history can be cleaned
Require pull requests with at least one approval, including CODEOWNERS for sensitive paths
Require status checks (build, tests, quality gate, scans) to pass before merging
questions.explanation: Reviews and passing checks are enforceable controls. Bypasses and force pushes undermine traceability.

questions.scenario: A team keeps feature branches open for three to four weeks and spends two days resolving conflicts before every release.
questions.question: Which practice addresses the root cause?
options: Assigning one person to do all merges
Trunk-based development: short-lived branches merged at least daily, with feature flags for unfinished work
Turning off CI on feature branches
Longer release cycles
questions.explanation: Conflict size grows with branch age. Integrating small changes frequently keeps conflicts small and main releasable.

questions.scenario: You need to write a commit message for a change that adds webhook signature verification to the payments module.
questions.question: Which message follows Conventional Commits and good practice?
options: updated code
feat(payments): verify HMAC-SHA512 signature on gateway webhooks (with a body explaining why and the ticket reference)
Fixed stuff in payments and other places
WIP
questions.explanation: A typed, scoped, imperative subject plus a body with the reason and ticket makes history searchable and enables automated changelogs.
